unit.unitOverview: Say that you arranged for something to be done, rather than that you did it. Read a clause twice: once for what it says and once for what it quietly requires of you. The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an account of a costly clause, a guide for small firms, and a set of supply terms.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.

Work out what a set of terms actually obliges you to do

visual.lectureScript:
Welcome to Stage 9, the last stretch of this course.
This unit is about money and about being a customer, and it starts with a form you have never met, which describes almost everything a customer actually does.

Think about what happens when your boiler breaks.
You do not repair it. You find somebody, you pay them, and they repair it.
If you say I repaired my boiler, that is not true, and English has a form that says the real thing in four words.
I had the boiler serviced.
Have, then the THING, then the past participle. That is the causative, and it is new.
The word order is where everything turns, and it is worth slowing down for.
I had the boiler serviced means somebody else did it.
I had serviced the boiler is a past perfect, from Unit 9, and it means you did the work yourself, earlier.
Same four words. Move the thing and you change who did the job.
Get does the same work, less formally. I got the boiler serviced. We need to get it looked at.
And it covers unwanted things too. We had our order cancelled without notice.

The second card puts a PERSON in the middle instead of a thing, and here the two forms diverge.
Get takes to. I got them to replace it.
Have does not. I had the engineer look at it.
Make and let do not either. They made me pay the surcharge. They let me keep the old one.
There is one small oddity worth knowing. Make gets its to back in the passive.
They made me pay, but I was made TO pay.

The third card is a reading skill more than a writing one, and the reading in this unit exists to make you take it seriously.
A firm lost about eleven hundred pounds to a clause four words long.
Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days.
They opened two boxes in December that had arrived in October, found defective seals, and had no claim at all.
The writer says they had thought deemed meant something like considered, which sounds arguable.
It is not arguable. In an agreement, deemed means the contract has decided, and the facts do not come into it.
That clause never says inspect your delivery. What it does is make not inspecting expensive.
So there is a habit worth having, and it is the whole card.
Read every passive clause twice. Once for what it says, and once for what it therefore requires you to do.
Is deemed. Is entitled to. Is liable for. Is rendered void. Is payable.
Each of those states a consequence, and most of them hide a requirement inside it.
And one of them does not, which matters just as much. Is entitled to gives you a right rather than a duty, and a right you never exercise is usually lost anyway.

The fourth card is about measuring things you cannot count, and it has one rule in it that catches almost everybody.
A portion is a part. A proportion is a share of the whole. A fraction of is not a measurement at all: it just means far less.
And here is the rule. The verb agrees with the noun after OF, not with the measure word.
A proportion of the batch was defective. A proportion of the items were defective.
The only thing that changed is the noun after of, and the verb followed it.

The last card finishes the comparisons. You have built four kinds across this level, and this is the shape a price list runs on.
The more you order, the lower the price.
Two things moving together, and both halves take the word the.
The sooner you report it, the better. The longer you leave it, the harder it becomes.
It can get very short. The sooner, the better.
The error is dropping one of the two the words, and the frame stops working the moment you do.

One last thing about this unit's vocabulary.
Markup and margin are two different numbers for the same money, and people use them interchangeably to your cost.
Compensation is for your loss, a refund is for the price, and reimbursement is for what you spent.
An ombudsman will usually not look at anything until you have complained to the firm first and given them time to reply.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: Fourteen Days
readings.setting: A small firm, after a delivery dispute
readings.passageScript:
We lost about eleven hundred pounds to a clause nobody had read, and it was four words long.
Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days.
The delivery came in October and we did not open two of the six boxes until December.
When we did, four of the seals in one batch were defective.
The supplier was perfectly polite about it and completely immovable.
After fourteen days the goods counted as accepted, whether we had looked at them or not.
That is what deemed means, and I did not know it.
I had thought it meant something like considered, as in we consider them accepted, which sounds arguable.
It is not arguable. It means the contract has decided, and the facts do not come into it.
What I do now takes about ten minutes per delivery.
I have every delivery checked on the day it arrives, and I have the checker sign the note.
I did not used to have anything checked. I opened boxes when I needed what was in them.
The eleven hundred pounds bought me a habit, which is an expensive way to acquire one.

readings.title: What a Contract Means by Deemed
readings.setting: A page from a guide for small firms
readings.passageScript:
A handful of words in an agreement do not mean what they mean in ordinary English.
The most dangerous is deemed.
In ordinary use, to deem something is to judge it, and a judgement can be argued with.
In an agreement, deemed means the contract treats it as true, and the facts are not relevant.
Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days does not mean somebody will decide whether you accepted them.
It means that on day fifteen they are accepted, whatever happened.
Three others are worth knowing.
Entitled to gives you a right, and a right you do not exercise is often lost.
Liable for imposes a cost, and it usually applies however the damage occurred.
Rendered void means an agreement stops counting, and it is almost always triggered by something you do.
There is a habit that protects you from all four.
Read every passive clause twice. Once for what it says, and once for what it therefore requires you to do.
Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days says nothing about you at all.
What it requires is that you inspect within fourteen days, and it never says so.

grammar.title: I had the boiler serviced: getting somebody else to do it
grammar.explanation:
This is new, and it describes most of what a customer actually does.
You do not repair the boiler. You arrange for somebody to repair it, and
English has a form that says exactly that in four words.
Without it, learners say I repaired my boiler, which claims they did it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
HAVE + the thing + the past participle

I had the boiler serviced.       (somebody serviced it for me)
We had the invoice checked.
She is having the unit replaced next week.
They had two of the seals tested.

GET does the same job, slightly less formally:
I got the boiler serviced.
We need to get it looked at.

The word order is fixed and it is where errors happen:
have + THING + PARTICIPLE, never have + participle + thing.
NOT: I had serviced the boiler. That is a past perfect and means I did it.

It works in any tense:
I will have it repaired.   I have had it repaired.   I am having it repaired.

And it covers things you did not want either:
We had our order cancelled without notice.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You paid an engineer to service your boiler. Say it.
1. Did you do the work? No. So I serviced the boiler is false.
2. The causative puts the THING straight after have: the boiler.
3. Then the past participle: serviced.
Answer: I had the boiler serviced.
I had serviced the boiler is a completely different sentence: it is a past
perfect, and it says you did the work yourself, earlier.
grammar.commonMistake:
The word order separates a causative from a past perfect, and nothing else does.
I had the boiler serviced  = somebody else did it.
I had serviced the boiler  = I did it, before something else.
Same four words. The position of the thing decides which sentence it is.
grammar.memoryTip: have + THING + the -ed form. Put the thing in the middle or the meaning flips.
grammar.practice:

grammar.title: I got them to replace it: making a person do something
grammar.explanation:
The card before this one puts the THING in the middle. This one puts the
PERSON there, and it says you persuaded, paid or required somebody to act.
The two look alike and take different forms after the middle word, which is
the whole difficulty.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
GET + PERSON + TO + plain verb
I got them to replace it.
We got the supplier to waive the surcharge.

HAVE + PERSON + plain verb, with NO to. More formal, and less common:
I had the engineer look at it.
We had the office send a copy.

So the two causatives differ in the middle AND in what follows:
have + THING  + PARTICIPLE      I had the unit replaced.
get  + PERSON + TO + verb       I got them to replace it.
have + PERSON + verb            I had them replace it.

MAKE and LET take no to either:
They made me pay the surcharge.   (I had no choice)
They let me keep the old one.     (they permitted it)
But in the PASSIVE, make gets its to back:
I was made TO pay the surcharge.

the point of mentioning three phone calls at all.

grammar.title: Is deemed, is entitled, is liable: the passive of an agreement
grammar.explanation:
You have built the passive for a production line, for a rule and across every
tense. A contract uses it for something else again: to state who owes what,
without naming anybody, so the clause holds whoever signs it.
You need to read these long before you need to write them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IS DEEMED = is treated as, whether or not it is true
  Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days.
IS ENTITLED TO = has a right to
  The customer is entitled to a replacement or a refund.
IS LIABLE FOR = must pay for
  The hirer is liable for any damage.
IS REQUIRED TO = must
  The supplier is required to notify us in writing.
IS RENDERED = is made
  The warranty is rendered void by unauthorised repair.
IS PAYABLE = must be paid
  The balance is payable within thirty days.

Two of these carry traps.
DEEMED means the contract decides, regardless of the facts. If goods are
deemed accepted after fourteen days, then on day fifteen they are accepted
even if nobody looked at them.
ENTITLED TO takes a noun or an -ing form: entitled to a refund, entitled to
cancel. Never entitled for.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.

actually require of you?
1. deemed means the contract treats them as accepted.
2. It does not say you must check them. It says what happens if you do not.
3. So the requirement is hidden: you must inspect within fourteen days.
Answer: you have fourteen days to find and report any fault.
After that the goods count as accepted whether you looked or not.
grammar.commonMistake:
These clauses state a consequence and hide the requirement inside it.
Goods are deemed accepted after fourteen days does not read like an
instruction, and it is one. Read every passive clause twice: once for what
it says, and once for what it therefore requires you to do.

6. The balance is payable within thirty days.

grammar.answerKey:
1. Inspect and report faults within fourteen days, or lose the right to.
2. Nothing. This one gives a right rather than imposing a duty.
3. Pay for damage, however it occurred.
4. Nothing of the customer. This one binds the supplier.
5. Do not have it repaired by anybody unauthorised.
6. Pay within thirty days.
7. entitled TO a refund.
Numbers 2 and 4 are the point: not every clause is a duty on you.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: A batch of, a proportion of: measuring what has no number
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you a few packets and a little flour, and a crowd and a flock.
A contract or an invoice needs a wider set, and it needs you to be exact
about whether you are describing a part, a share or a comparison.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
A PART, with no claim about the whole:
a portion of the order      a batch of seals
a bundle of cables          a quantity of stock

A SHARE, measured against the whole:
a proportion of the batch   a percentage of the total
two thirds of the delivery  the majority of the items

A COMPARISON dressed as a measurement:
a fraction of the cost      a tiny percentage
These sound precise and are not. a fraction of just means far less.

THE VERB agrees with what follows OF, not with the measure word:
A proportion of the batch WAS defective.   (batch is singular)
A proportion of the items WERE defective.  (items are plural)
That rule catches almost everybody.

AND THE PAIR TO KEEP APART:
a portion of  = a part, absolute
a proportion of = a share, relative to the whole

grammar.title: The more you order, the lower the price
grammar.explanation:
Three units have built comparisons for you: Unit 3 gave you not as quickly
as, Unit 10 the irregulars, Unit 14 the multiples.

moving together.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
THE + comparative, THE + comparative

The more you order, the lower the price.
The sooner you report it, the better.
The longer you leave it, the harder it becomes.
The more often it is checked, the fewer faults are found.

Both halves take THE, and the comparative comes straight after it.
Note what is missing: there is no that and usually no comma problem — the
comma between the halves is required.

The second half can be very short:
The sooner, the better.
The less said, the better.

AND THE AMOUNT-COMPARISON that goes with it:
It costs a fraction of the original quote.
The margin is narrower on that line than on this one.
Prices rise in proportion to the quantity.

A warning carried from Unit 14: every comparison invites the question
compared with what, and a price comparison invites it twice as hard.

assignments.title: The terms, and the letter that relies on them
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write eight lines of supply terms for a business you invent.
Use is payable, is deemed, is entitled to, is liable for and is rendered void, one each.
Include one tolerance clause with a percentage, and finish with a paired comparison.
No clause may have we, I or you as its subject.
Part two. Beside each clause, write one line saying what it requires of the customer.
At least one must require nothing.
Part three. Now write a customer's letter, about 160 words, pursuing a remedy under
your own terms. Use at least two causatives. Give at least two figures, one of which
concedes something you are NOT claiming. Cite a clause by number. Say what you will
do next, with a date.
Part four. Write the supplier's best reply in three sentences, then the one sentence
you would add to your letter to close it off.
